subject: film
title: New German Cinema, 1962 to 1982
dek: On 28 February 1962, twenty-six young West German filmmakers stood up at a short-film festival in Oberhausen and declared that the old cinema was dead. Out of that protest, and out of later public funding and television money, came a generation of directors — Fassbinder, Herzog, Wenders, Schlöndorff, von Trotta and many others — whose low-budget films brought German cinema back to international attention for the first time since the Weimar years. This lesson covers how the movement started, what the films were about, who made them, and what else was happening in world cinema at the same time.
era: c. 1962 to 1982, with roots in 1950s West German popular cinema and a short look at what followed
honesty: This lesson keeps to facts documented in the English Wikipedia articles on New German Cinema, the Oberhausen Manifesto, the films and the directors, and in festival records from Cannes, Venice, Berlin and the Academy Awards. The wording of the manifesto was checked against the Museum of Modern Art's 2012 presentation of the text. Where a detail could not be checked, it was left out. There are no images today rather than risk pictures that do not match their captions.

timeline.label: Heimatfilme fill the cinemas
timeline.detail: West German screens are dominated by commercially safe rural melodramas, comedies and musicals. Serious reckoning with the Nazi past is rare in popular cinema.

timeline.label: A prize with no winner
timeline.detail: No West German film is judged worthy of the Federal Film Prize. The interior minister describes a short, shallow flowering of tear-jerking entertainment.

timeline.label: The Oberhausen Manifesto
timeline.detail: On 28 February, at the International Short Film Festival Oberhausen, twenty-six filmmakers issue a short declaration calling for a new German feature film, free from industry conventions and commercial control.

timeline.label: The Kuratorium is created
timeline.detail: The Federal Interior Ministry sets up the Kuratorium junger deutscher Film to fund first features by emerging directors.

timeline.label: Yesterday Girl and Young Törless
timeline.detail: Alexander Kluge's Yesterday Girl wins a special jury prize at Venice. Volker Schlöndorff releases Young Törless. Film schools open in West Berlin and Munich around this time.

timeline.label: A federal film board
timeline.detail: The government creates the Filmförderungsanstalt, a body to support filmmaking in West Germany.

timeline.label: Fassbinder's first feature
timeline.detail: Rainer Werner Fassbinder, coming out of Munich theatre, releases Love Is Colder Than Death. Katzelmacher follows the same year.

timeline.label: Filmverlag der Autoren
timeline.detail: Directors form their own production and distribution company. Rosa von Praunheim releases It Is Not the Homosexual Who Is Perverse, But the Society in Which He Lives.

timeline.label: Aguirre, the Wrath of God
timeline.detail: Werner Herzog and Klaus Kinski film a Spanish expedition going to pieces on the Amazon. The film becomes Herzog's international breakthrough.

timeline.label: Film and television make a deal
timeline.detail: ARD, ZDF and the federal film board agree that television money can support films that play in cinemas first, and may appear on television only twenty-four months later. Fassbinder's Ali: Fear Eats the Soul and Wim Wenders's Alice in the Cities are released. Helke Sander founds the journal Frauen und Film.

timeline.label: The Lost Honour of Katharina Blum
timeline.detail: Schlöndorff and Margarethe von Trotta adapt Heinrich Böll's novel about a woman destroyed by police and press after a brief encounter with a wanted man.

timeline.label: German Autumn on film
timeline.detail: After the kidnappings and deaths of autumn 1977, Kluge, Fassbinder, Schlöndorff and others make the collective film Germany in Autumn, released in 1978.

timeline.label: The Tin Drum and Maria Braun
timeline.detail: Schlöndorff's The Tin Drum shares the Palme d'Or at Cannes with Apocalypse Now. Fassbinder's The Marriage of Maria Braun becomes his greatest popular success.

timeline.label: An Oscar, and a fifteen-hour novel
timeline.detail: The Tin Drum wins the Academy Award for Best Foreign Language Film, the first German film to do so. Fassbinder's television adaptation of Berlin Alexanderplatz is broadcast.

timeline.label: A Golden Lion for von Trotta
timeline.detail: Marianne and Juliane (Die bleierne Zeit) wins the Golden Lion at Venice. Von Trotta is the first woman to receive the award.

timeline.label: An ending, and two late peaks
timeline.detail: Fassbinder dies in Munich on 10 June, aged 37. His death is often treated as the end of the movement's main period. The same year, Veronika Voss wins the Golden Bear in Berlin, and Herzog's Fitzcarraldo wins Best Director at Cannes.

timeline.label: Paris, Texas
timeline.detail: Wenders's Paris, Texas, made after the usual 1962–1982 dates, wins the Palme d'Or at Cannes. German cinema's international reputation does not vanish with Fassbinder.

fun_fact.title: The slogan that is not in the manifesto
fun_fact.text: The phrase everyone associates with Oberhausen is 'Papas Kino ist tot' — 'Papa's cinema is dead.' It was the title of the press conference at which the manifesto was read, on 28 February 1962, but it does not appear in the manifesto itself. The text, about 150 words in German, ends with a different line: 'Der alte Film ist tot. Wir glauben an den neuen' — 'The old film is dead. We believe in the new one.'

sections.title: Papa's cinema, and a different Germany from Weimar

blocks.text: This is not the Germany of German Expressionism (c. 1919–1931), the painted studios and anxious shadows of Weimar that this site has already covered. By the 1950s that cinema, and the people who had made it, had been scattered by exile, war and the division of the country. West German cinemas in the Adenauer years were full of Heimatfilme, rural melodramas set in tidy landscapes, along with comedies and musicals that did good business and asked little of the audience. The Nazi years were not absent from every film, but they were rarely faced in a sustained way.

East Germany had a different system altogether: a state studio, DEFA, and directors such as Konrad Wolf working inside it. New German Cinema, the subject of this lesson, is a West German story. The two industries barely shared a public, a funding model or a language of criticism.

The crisis of the commercial industry became hard to ignore in 1961, when no West German film was judged worthy of the Federal Film Prize. The federal interior minister spoke of a short, shallow flowering of tear-jerking entertainment. Young short-film directors, some of them already winning prizes at international festivals, had a ready answer: the old industry could not, or would not, make the films they wanted to make.

sections.title: 28 February 1962: a short text and a long aftermath

blocks.text: The International Short Film Festival Oberhausen, in North Rhine-Westphalia, was where this discontent found a public form. On 28 February 1962 a loose group known as DOC 59 held a press conference titled 'Papas Kino ist tot.' Ferdinand Khittl read a short manifesto. Alexander Kluge chaired the discussion that followed. The declaration had been initiated by Haro Senft. Twenty-six people signed it: directors, cinematographers, producers and one composer. Among them were Kluge, Edgar Reitz, Peter Schamoni, Herbert Vesely, Hansjürgen Pohland and Detten Schleiermacher.

The text itself is brief. It says that the collapse of conventional German film has removed the economic basis for a mentality the signatories reject, and that recent German short films, already recognised at international festivals, show that the future lies with people who speak a new film language. It demands freedom from the conventions of the established industry, from commercial partners, and from control by special interest groups. It ends: 'Der alte Film ist tot. Wir glauben an den neuen.' The signatories say they have concrete intellectual, formal and economic ideas, and that they are prepared to take economic risks.

The manifesto did not contain a production plan. What it did was put pressure on cultural policy. In 1965 the Federal Interior Ministry created the Kuratorium junger deutscher Film, a fund for first features. Film schools followed: Kluge, Schleiermacher and Reitz helped found the Institut für Filmgestaltung at Ulm; the Deutsche Film- und Fernsehakademie Berlin opened in 1966; the Hochschule für Fernsehen und Film in Munich was established in 1966 and opened in 1967. The early years are sometimes called Young German Cinema, to mark a more austere, experimental phase before the more widely seen films of the 1970s.

sections.title: What the new films were like

blocks.text: The directors did not share one style. What they shared was a condition of work: low budgets, personal control over the script and the shoot, and a wish to look at West German life rather than at a smoothed-down version of it. They took formal ideas from the French New Wave (c. 1958–64) and from Italian Neorealism (c. 1943–1952), and they also borrowed freely from Hollywood genres — the gangster film, the melodrama, the road movie — and then twisted them.

items: Authorship. The director was expected to write, or closely control, the film. The German word often used is Autorenfilm: a film whose author is the director.

Subjects close to hand. Guest workers, unhappy marriages, small-town boredom, the economic miracle and its costs, American popular culture, and, again and again, the Nazi past and what the parents' generation had done or failed to do.

A home audience that was often smaller than the foreign one. Many of these films found their first serious praise at festivals and in art houses abroad, and only later, or never, became popular in West German cinemas.

Television as a partner and a problem. Until 1974, broadcasters who put money into a film often wanted a television premiere first, which hurt the film's chances in cinemas. The Film-Fernseh-Abkommen of 1974, an agreement between ARD, ZDF and the federal film board created in 1968, reserved an annual sum for films that would play in theatres first and reach television only after twenty-four months.

blocks.text: In 1971 a group of directors formed Filmverlag der Autoren, their own production and distribution company. It became, for much of the 1970s, the practical home of the movement. The work still depended on subsidies. A 1977 report in the New York Times put the typical subsidy share of a West German film budget at 80 percent.

The first features that critics treated as proof of the manifesto's promise included Kluge's Yesterday Girl (1966), about a young East German woman adrift in the West, which won a special jury prize at the Venice Film Festival, and Schlöndorff's Young Törless (1966), adapted from Robert Musil. Reitz, a signatory, made Mahlzeiten the same year. Herbert Vesely had already filmed Heinrich Böll's The Bread of Those Early Years in 1962.

Around them gathered a larger group who had not all signed the manifesto but worked in the same world: Fassbinder, Herzog, Wenders, Hans-Jürgen Syberberg, Werner Schroeter, the partnership of Jean-Marie Straub and Danièle Huillet, Peter Fleischmann, Harun Farocki, and, from the mid-1970s, a group of women directors whose work was for a long time treated as a side chapter and should not be. Helma Sanders-Brahms made Germany Pale Mother (1980). Helke Sander, from the first class at the Berlin film academy, organised a women's film seminar in Berlin in 1973 with Claudia von Alemann and in 1974 founded Frauen und Film, the first feminist film journal in Europe. Ulrike Ottinger made formally adventurous films that sit in both this movement and the history of women's cinema. Rosa von Praunheim's 1971 film It Is Not the Homosexual Who Is Perverse, But the Society in Which He Lives is a founding document of the postwar German lesbian and gay movement.
The next sections go deeper on three directors whose names travelled furthest, and then on two films that took major festival prizes in the movement's last years.

sections.title: Fassbinder: more than forty films, and then a stop

blocks.text: Rainer Werner Fassbinder was born in Bad Wörishofen on 31 May 1945 and died in Munich on 10 June 1982, at the age of 37. He came to film through theatre. In Munich he led the Action-Theatre and then the Anti-Theater, and he brought a regular company of actors with him onto the set, among them Hanna Schygulla and Irm Hermann. He was turned down by the Berlin film school. He made his first feature, Love Is Colder Than Death, in 1969, and he barely slowed down afterwards. In about fifteen years he completed more than forty films and television dramas, including the serials World on a Wire (1973) and Berlin Alexanderplatz (1980), the latter a more than thirteen-hour adaptation of Alfred Döblin's 1929 novel.

The early films are spare, often shot with a still camera, and close to his stage work: Katzelmacher (1969) watches a group of bored young people turn on a Greek guest worker. In the early 1970s he turned toward Hollywood melodrama, especially the 1950s films of Douglas Sirk, and used that style to look at everyday cruelty — in families, in marriages, and in a society that had not finished with its past. The Merchant of Four Seasons (1972) was his first commercial success at home. Ali: Fear Eats the Soul (1974), made quickly and cheaply, was his international breakthrough. An older German cleaning woman marries a younger Moroccan worker; the people around them insult, isolate and then, when it suits them, tolerate the couple. The film won the International Critics' Prize at Cannes.

The Marriage of Maria Braun (1979), with Schygulla in the title role, was his greatest popular success. A woman builds a life and a career in the years of the economic miracle while the husband she married at the end of the war remains out of reach. The film is the first of a loose trilogy about women in postwar West Germany, completed by Lola (1981) and Veronika Voss (1982), which won the Golden Bear at the Berlin International Film Festival shortly before Fassbinder's death. He died of a combination of cocaine and barbiturates. His death is often treated as the end of New German Cinema's main period.

sections.title: Herzog and Wenders: the river and the road

blocks.text: Werner Herzog, born in Munich in 1942 and raised for a time in a remote Bavarian village, made films about people who push themselves, or are pushed, past ordinary limits, often in landscapes that seem to resist them. His first feature, Signs of Life (1968), won a Silver Bear in Berlin. Aguirre, the Wrath of God (1972), shot on the Amazon with Klaus Kinski as a Spanish soldier who loses his hold on reality while chasing a rumoured city of gold, made his international name. The Enigma of Kaspar Hauser (1974) won the Grand Prix at Cannes. Fitzcarraldo (1982), in which a character tries to haul a steamship over a hill in the Peruvian Amazon in order to build an opera house, was as demanding to shoot as its plot suggests; Herzog won the Best Director prize at Cannes that year.

A story from 1974 shows how he thought about loyalty and will. When the film historian Lotte H. Eisner, a mentor who had fled the Nazis, fell seriously ill in Paris, Herzog walked from Munich to Paris, a journey of three weeks, believing she would not die if he did so. He kept a diary, later published as Of Walking in Ice. Eisner lived until 1983.

Wim Wenders, born in Düsseldorf in 1945, studied at the new Munich film school and began as a critic before making features. With the cinematographer Robby Müller he built a loose road-movie trilogy: Alice in the Cities (1974), The Wrong Move (1975) and Kings of the Road (1976), the last of which won a FIPRESCI prize at Cannes. The films watch people who are not quite at home in West Germany, often with America as a dream, a soundtrack or a destination. The American Friend (1977), adapted from Patricia Highsmith and starring Dennis Hopper and Bruno Ganz, brought that tension into a thriller. After the usual end-date of the movement, Paris, Texas (1984) won the Palme d'Or, and Wings of Desire (1987), with Ganz as an angel in Berlin, won Best Director at Cannes. Those later films belong to the afterlife of New German Cinema, not to its first run, but they are part of why the names still travel.

sections.title: The Tin Drum, and two sisters in a leaden time

blocks.text: Volker Schlöndorff had been making features since Young Törless. In 1975 he and Margarethe von Trotta, then his partner in work and in life, directed The Lost Honour of Katharina Blum, from Heinrich Böll's novel about a woman whose life is torn apart by the police and the tabloid press. In 1979 Schlöndorff adapted Günter Grass's The Tin Drum. A boy born in Danzig in the 1920s decides, at the age of three, to stop growing, and he watches the rise of Nazism with a toy drum and a scream that can shatter glass. The film shared the 1979 Palme d'Or with Francis Ford Coppola's Apocalypse Now — the first Palme d'Or for a film by a German director — and in 1980 it became the first German film to win the Academy Award for Best Foreign Language Film.

Von Trotta's Marianne and Juliane (Die bleierne Zeit, 1981) follows two sisters, daughters of a pastor, whose lives diverge after the 1960s. Juliane works at a feminist magazine and tries to change the country by legal means. Marianne has gone into the armed underground. The film is loosely based on the lives of Christiane and Gudrun Ensslin, and it is dedicated to Christiane. It puts the years of the Red Army Faction in the longer setting of a strict postwar childhood and an unmastered Nazi past. At the 1981 Venice Film Festival it won the Golden Lion. Von Trotta was the first woman to receive that prize.

sections.title: What else was happening at the same time

blocks.text: The Oberhausen date, 1962, sits in a crowded decade of 'new' cinemas. The French New Wave (c. 1958–64) was already in full force when the manifesto was read, and it was an acknowledged model: personal films, shot quickly, often in real places. Italian Neorealism (c. 1943–1952) was older, but its habit of taking the camera into ordinary streets still mattered. In Czechoslovakia, The Czechoslovak New Wave was unfolding in the same years, until the Soviet-led invasion of 1968 closed much of it down. In Brazil, Cinema Novo was arguing that a poor country needed a cinema that showed hunger rather than gloss. In the United States, New Hollywood (c. 1967–1980) was giving a generation of directors unusual freedom inside the studios, a very different economic world from the subsidy-dependent West German one.

A little later, and on the other side of the world, Taiwan New Cinema (c. 1982–1990s) and China's Fifth Generation filmmakers, 1982 to 1994, would also make their names at foreign festivals with films that looked unlike the official cinema at home. The parallel is real and should not be stretched too far. Each of these movements had its own political conditions, its own money, and its own arguments. What they share is a pattern: a group of directors, often trained together or funded by a new public mechanism, using a moment of institutional looseness to put a country's recent history and everyday life on screen, and finding that the first loud applause sometimes comes from abroad.

Fassbinder's death did not end anyone else's career. Wenders and Herzog kept working, and still do. Reitz's long television chronicle Heimat appeared in 1984. Some directors moved toward larger, more international productions; some of those films failed commercially, which is one reason the movement is usually closed in the early 1980s. A later group of German filmmakers, often called the Berlin School, emerged in the 1990s and 2000s with a quieter, observational style. They are a subsequent generation, not a continuation under the same name.

What remains from 1962 to 1982 is a body of films that returned German cinema to international critical life for the first time since Weimar, and a record of how one country's artists tried to look at prosperity, guilt, gender, migration and political violence without smoothing them away. The manifesto had promised a new film. The films that followed did not form a single school. They did, for two decades, make it possible to speak of a new German cinema and be understood outside Germany.

Many of these films are about a younger generation trying to live with a national past that the people who raised them had not fully faced. If you think about films, books or family stories from Taiwan after martial law, what do they do with an unprocessed past — name it, circle it, or leave it just off screen? What would count, for you, as facing it honestly?

glossary.explain: The period in West German cinema, usually dated 1962 to 1982, in which a new generation of directors made low-budget, author-driven films that won international attention.
A name sometimes used for the more austere, experimental West German films of the 1960s, before the more widely seen work of the 1970s.

A short declaration signed by 26 filmmakers on 28 February 1962 at the International Short Film Festival Oberhausen, calling for a new German feature film free from industry conventions and commercial control.
German for 'Papa's cinema is dead.' It was the title of the 28 February 1962 press conference at Oberhausen, but the phrase does not appear in the manifesto itself.
A commercially popular West German film genre of the 1950s, usually a sentimental story set in a tidy rural landscape.
A funding body created in 1965 by the Federal Interior Ministry to support first features by emerging West German directors.
A government body created in 1968 to support filmmaking in West Germany, often abbreviated FFA.

A 1974 agreement between the public broadcasters ARD and ZDF and the federal film board, providing television money for films that would play in cinemas first and reach television only after 24 months.
A production and distribution company founded by West German directors in 1971, which funded and released many New German Cinema films.
A film conceived as the work of a director-author, who typically writes or closely controls the script as well as the shooting.
The state-owned film studio of East Germany, a separate industry from the West German cinema described in this lesson.
West Germany's main state film prize, the Bundesfilmpreis. In 1961 no domestic film was awarded it.
A loose alliance of short-film directors out of which the Oberhausen Manifesto press conference was organised.
A film school founded in 1962 at the Hochschule für Gestaltung Ulm by Alexander Kluge, Detten Schleiermacher and Edgar Reitz.

A later group of German filmmakers, active from the 1990s and 2000s, with a quieter observational style; a subsequent generation, not part of New German Cinema itself.
The rapid West German postwar recovery, the Wirtschaftswunder, often dated from the 1950s into the 1960s.
Konrad Adenauer, chancellor of West Germany from 1949 to 1963. The 'Adenauer years' here means the conservative postwar period of reconstruction and official quiet about the Nazi past.

glossary.explain: Fassbinder's 1972 film, with an all-woman cast, about a fashion designer and the people she loves and controls.
Fassbinder's 1973 science-fiction television film about a simulated world, later an influence on later films about artificial reality.
Fassbinder's 1979 film, starring Hanna Schygulla, about a woman's rise during the West German economic miracle; his greatest popular success.
Fassbinder's 1981 film, the second in a loose trilogy about women in the economic-miracle years.
Fassbinder's 1982 film about a faded starlet in the 1950s; it won the Golden Bear at Berlin shortly before his death.
Fassbinder's 1980 television adaptation of Alfred Döblin's novel, more than thirteen hours long, about a man trying and failing to live straight in late-Weimar Berlin.
Fassbinder's 1975 film about a working-class gay man whose lottery win is used against him by a wealthier lover.
Fassbinder's 1978 film about the last days of a transgender woman; one of his most personal works.
A 1978 collective film, organised especially by Alexander Kluge, in which Fassbinder, Schlöndorff and others respond to the events of the German Autumn of 1977.
Herzog's first feature, from 1968, which won a Silver Bear at the Berlin International Film Festival.
Herzog's 1972 film, starring Klaus Kinski, about a Spanish expedition that unravels on the Amazon.
Herzog's 1974 film about a young man who appears in a town with almost no past; it won the Grand Prix at Cannes.
Herzog's 1982 film about a man determined to haul a steamship over a hill in the Amazon to build an opera house; Herzog won Best Director at Cannes.
Herzog's published diary of his 1974 walk from Munich to Paris to visit the ailing film historian Lotte H. Eisner.
Wenders's 1974 road film, the first of a loose trilogy, in which a journalist travels with a young girl.
Wenders's 1975 film, the middle part of his road trilogy.
Wenders's 1976 film about two men travelling along the East German border; it won a FIPRESCI prize at Cannes.
Wenders's 1977 thriller, adapted from Patricia Highsmith, starring Dennis Hopper and Bruno Ganz.
Wenders's 1984 film, made just after the usual dates of New German Cinema, which won the Palme d'Or at Cannes.
Wenders's 1987 film about angels in Berlin, for which he won Best Director at Cannes.

glossary.term: The Lost Honour of Katharina Blum
aliases: Die verlorene Ehre der Katharina Blum
glossary.explain: A 1975 film directed by Schlöndorff and von Trotta, from Heinrich Böll's novel about a woman destroyed by police and tabloid press.
Schlöndorff's 1979 adaptation of Günter Grass's novel; it shared the Palme d'Or and in 1980 became the first German film to win the Academy Award for Best Foreign Language Film.
Von Trotta's 1981 film about two sisters, one a journalist and one in the armed underground; it won the Golden Lion at Venice. German title: Die bleierne Zeit.
Helma Sanders-Brahms's 1980 film about a mother and daughter living through the war and the early Federal Republic.

glossary.term: It Is Not the Homosexual Who Is Perverse, But the Society in Which He Lives
glossary.explain: Rosa von Praunheim's 1971 film, a founding work of the postwar German lesbian and gay movement.
Hans-Jürgen Syberberg's 1977 film essay on Hitler and German culture.
Edgar Reitz's long television chronicle of a German village across the twentieth century, first broadcast in 1984, after the main period of New German Cinema.
A 1955 Hollywood melodrama by Douglas Sirk, a model for Fassbinder's Ali: Fear Eats the Soul.
Francis Ford Coppola's 1979 Vietnam War film, which shared the Palme d'Or with The Tin Drum.
Peter Fleischmann's 1969 film, often listed among key works of New German Cinema.
A labour migrant, in West German usage often a Gastarbeiter from southern Europe, Turkey or North Africa, who appears in films such as Katzelmacher and Ali: Fear Eats the Soul.
American actor (1936–2010) who starred in Wenders's The American Friend (1977).
West Germany's main public broadcasting consortium, one of the parties to the 1974 Film-Fernseh-Abkommen.
West Germany's second public television channel, one of the parties to the 1974 Film-Fernseh-Abkommen.
